title: Understanding Fractions
subject: Mathematics
description: Fractions as parts of a whole and of a set, numerators and denominators, unit/proper/improper/mixed and like/unlike fractions, converting between improper and mixed fractions, equivalent fractions, comparing and ordering like fractions, and adding/subtracting like fractions in word problems.

questions.question: When a whole is divided into equal parts, what is each equal part called?
questions.explanation: The book says: when a whole is divided into EQUAL parts, each equal part is called a fraction. Factors and multiples belong to multiplication, not to parts of a whole.

questions.question: In the fraction 3/7, which number is the numerator?
questions.explanation: The numerator is the numeral ABOVE the fractional bar, so in 3/7 it is 3. The 7 below the bar is the denominator. 10 (3 + 7) and 4 (7 - 3) are just sums and differences, not parts of the fraction.

questions.question: In the fraction 5/9, what does the denominator 9 tell us?
options: 9 of the parts are being considered
The whole is cut into 9 equal parts
The whole is cut into 9 unequal parts
questions.explanation: The denominator tells the TOTAL number of equal parts the whole is divided into (9). The numerator (5) tells how many of those parts are considered. Parts of a fraction must always be equal.

questions.question: What is the horizontal line between the numerator and the denominator called?
questions.explanation: The two numerals of a fraction are separated by a horizontal bar called the fractional bar. The book adds that it is also referred to as a vinculum - a line that shows numbers are bound together as a group.

questions.question: In a fraction, the numerator shows the total number of equal parts the whole is divided into.
questions.explanation: False - that is the job of the DENOMINATOR (the number below the bar). The numerator (above the bar) shows how many of the equal parts are being considered.

questions.question: A whole chikki is cut into 8 equal triangular pieces and you eat 2 of them. What fraction of the chikki did you eat?
questions.explanation: Pieces eaten (2) go on top, total equal pieces (8) go below: 2/8. 8/2 swaps the numbers, 6/8 is the part NOT eaten, and 2/6 wrongly uses the remaining pieces as the denominator.

questions.question: A chikki is cut into 9 equal square pieces and 4 pieces are eaten. What fraction of the chikki REMAINS?
questions.explanation: 9 - 4 = 5 pieces remain out of 9 equal pieces, so the remaining fraction is 5/9. 4/9 is the part eaten; 5/4 and 9/5 put the wrong number in the denominator - the denominator must stay 9 (total pieces).

questions.question: A friend says 4/9 means '4 wholes divided into 9'. What does 4/9 really mean?
options: 9 of the 4 equal parts of one whole
4 of the 9 equal parts of one whole
questions.explanation: A fraction is a part of ONE whole: the denominator 9 says the whole is cut into 9 equal parts and the numerator 4 says 4 of them are taken. Nothing is being 'put together' or shared among people.

questions.question: What special name does the fraction 1/2 have?
questions.explanation: The book says 1/2 has the special name 'half'. A quarter is 1/4, a third is 1/3, and a whole is 1 (or 2/2).

questions.question: One fourth (1/4) is also called ______.
questions.explanation: 1/4 is read as 'one fourth' and is also referred to as a quarter. Half is 1/2, a third is 1/3 and a whole is 4/4.

questions.question: Which of these is a unit fraction?
questions.explanation: A unit fraction has numerator 1 and a denominator greater than 1 - so 1/7 fits. 7/1 and 7/7 do not have 1 on top, and 2/7 has numerator 2.

questions.question: How is the fraction 5/17 written in words?
questions.explanation: Read the numerator as a counting number (five) and the denominator as an ordinal with -s (seventeenths): five seventeenths. 'Seventeen fifths' would be 17/5.

questions.question: Write 'seven halves' as a fraction.
questions.explanation: 'Halves' means the denominator is 2 and 'seven' is the numerator: 7/2. Notice this is an improper fraction (more than 1 whole) - that is allowed. 2/7 is 'two sevenths'.

questions.question: A fraction with 1 as its denominator, such as 5/1, is called a unit fraction.
questions.explanation: False. A unit fraction has 1 as its NUMERATOR (1/4, 1/7, 1/11 ...). The denominator is the one that must be greater than 1. This is Statement (II) of the worksheet's true/false item, and it is false.

questions.question: Select ALL the unit fractions in this list.
questions.explanation: Unit fractions have numerator 1: 1/5 and 1/9. 5/8 is proper but not unit; 9/6 and 10/7 are improper fractions.

questions.topic: Fraction as Part of a Whole
questions.question: A whole is divided into 3 equal parts. Which fraction represents the WHOLE?
questions.explanation: Each part is 1/3 and three one-thirds make the whole, written 3/3. The book shows this pattern for halves (2/2) and fourths (4/4) too.

questions.topic: Fraction as Part of a Whole
questions.question: How many one fourths (1/4) make a whole?
questions.explanation: Four one fourths make the whole: 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 4/4 = 1. The denominator tells you how many unit pieces fill the whole.

questions.topic: Fraction as Part of a Whole
questions.question: If 4/6 of a rectangle is shaded, what fraction is UNSHADED?
questions.explanation: The whole is 6/6. Unshaded = 6/6 - 4/6 = 2/6. Keep the denominator 6 - only the numerators change.

questions.topic: Fraction as Part of a Whole
questions.question: A paper strip of unit length is folded into 2 equal parts, then each part is folded into 2 again. Each small part is how long?
questions.explanation: Folding into 2 gives halves (1/2). Folding each half again gives 4 equal parts, each 1/4 of the strip. 2/4 would be TWO of those small parts.

questions.topic: Fraction as Part of a Whole
questions.question: Statement (I): The fraction 4/4 represents 4 whole units. Statement (II): The fraction 4/4 represents 1 whole unit. Select the correct option.
questions.explanation: Four one-fourths make ONE whole, so 4/4 = 1, not 4. Statement (I) is false and Statement (II) is true. A fraction equals as many wholes as the numerator has GROUPS of the denominator (4 ÷ 4 = 1).

questions.topic: Fraction as Part of a Whole
questions.question: Statement (I): 3 times 1/5 = 3/5. Statement (II): The fraction 5/5 represents 5 wholes. Select the correct option.
questions.explanation: 3 times 1/5 is 1/5 + 1/5 + 1/5 = 3/5, so (I) is true. But 5/5 means five one-fifths, which together make exactly ONE whole, so (II) is false.

questions.topic: Fraction as Part of a Whole
questions.question: A pancake is cut into 4 equal pieces. 3 times 1/4 equals:
questions.explanation: 3 times 1/4 = 3/4. Since only 3 of the 4 pieces are taken, this is less than one whole pancake. You need 4 times 1/4 = 4/4 to make 1.

questions.question: To show 3/7 on a number line, into how many equal parts should the gap between 0 and 1 be divided?
questions.explanation: Divide the part between 0 and 1 into as many equal parts as the DENOMINATOR (7). Then count 3 of those parts from 0 to reach 3/7.

questions.question: A number line in thirteenths reads 1/13, 2/13, 3/13, ___, 5/13. What is the missing fraction?
questions.explanation: The marks go up by one thirteenth each time, so after 3/13 comes 4/13. The denominator stays 13 on the whole line.

questions.question: A number line in twelfths reads 8/12, ___, 10/12, 11/12. What is the missing fraction?
questions.explanation: Between 8/12 and 10/12 lies 9/12. All marks on this line are twelfths, so the denominator must remain 12.

questions.question: On a number line marked in halves (1/2, 2/2, 3/2 ...) from 0 to 4, where exactly does 8/2 sit?
questions.explanation: Two halves make 1, so 8 halves make 8 ÷ 2 = 4. The fraction 8/2 sits exactly on the whole number 4 at the end of the line.

questions.question: Which of these fractions lies to the RIGHT of 1 on a number line?
questions.explanation: 7/4 is an improper fraction (numerator 7 > denominator 4), so it is more than one whole and sits past 1. 3/4, 1/4 and 1/2 are proper fractions between 0 and 1.

questions.question: On a number line, the fraction farther to the right is the greater fraction.
questions.explanation: True. Numbers grow as you move right, so 5/2 (farther right) is greater than 3/2. The book uses this to compare like fractions.

questions.question: Between 0 and 1 on a number line, where does 5/6 sit compared with 2/6 and 4/6?
questions.explanation: On a line in sixths, 5/6 is the fifth mark - after 2/6 and after 4/6 - so it lies to the right of both, just one mark before 6/6 = 1.

questions.question: A set has 12 cars. How many cars is 1/2 of the set?
questions.explanation: Divide the set into 2 equal parts: 12 ÷ 2 = 6. So 1/2 of 12 cars = 6 cars. (4 would be 1/3 and 3 would be 1/4 of 12.)

questions.question: How many cars is 2/3 of a set of 12 cars?
questions.explanation: First find 1/3 of 12 = 12 ÷ 3 = 4. Then 2/3 is 2 times that: 2 × 4 = 8 cars. (6 is 1/2 of 12 and 9 is 3/4 of 12.)

questions.question: 3/4 of 12 cars = 3 times (1/4 of 12). How many cars is that?
questions.explanation: 1/4 of 12 = 12 ÷ 4 = 3 cars. Then 3/4 = 3 × 3 = 9 cars. 12 would be 4/4 (the whole set).

questions.question: There are 7 colour pencils and 2 of them are red. What fraction of the pencils is NOT red?
questions.explanation: The whole set is 7 pencils. Red = 2/7, so not red = 7 - 2 = 5 pencils out of 7 = 5/7. The denominator stays 7 (the whole set).

questions.question: 18 roses are shared equally among 3 vases. How many roses are in 2/3 of the whole?
questions.explanation: 1/3 of 18 = 18 ÷ 3 = 6 roses (one vase). 2/3 = 2 × 6 = 12 roses (two vases). 3/3 would be all 18.

questions.question: There are 12 flowers. Two thirds are coloured pink and one fourth are coloured orange. What fraction of the flowers remains uncoloured?
questions.explanation: 2/3 of 12 = 8 pink; 1/4 of 12 = 3 orange. Coloured = 8 + 3 = 11, so 12 - 11 = 1 flower is left: 1/12 of the flowers.

questions.question: There are 8 stars. Two fourths are coloured yellow and two eighths blue. What fraction of the stars stays uncoloured?
questions.explanation: 2/4 of 8 = 4 yellow stars; 2/8 of 8 = 2 blue stars. Coloured = 6, so 8 - 6 = 2 stars remain: 2/8 of the stars.

questions.question: 1/4 of 12 is 3, so 3/4 of 12 is 9.
questions.explanation: True. Once you know one fourth of 12 is 3, three fourths is three of those: 3 × 3 = 9.

questions.question: Which of these is a PROPER fraction?
questions.explanation: A proper fraction has a numerator SMALLER than its denominator: 9 < 11, so 9/11 is proper. 11/9, 9/9 and 11/7 have numerators equal to or bigger than the denominator - they are improper.

questions.question: Improper fractions represent amounts that are:
options: equal to or more than a whole
questions.explanation: Improper fractions have numerator greater than OR equal to the denominator, e.g. 7/4, 5/2, 9/9. So they are equal to or more than a whole.

questions.question: A fraction whose numerator equals its denominator, such as 7/7, is a proper fraction.
questions.explanation: False. Proper fractions need the numerator to be LESS than the denominator. When they are equal (7/7 = 1 whole) the fraction is improper.

questions.question: In a mixed fraction such as 2 1/2, the fractional part must be:
questions.explanation: A mixed fraction is a whole part plus a fractional part that is LESS than one (a proper fraction). It need not be a unit fraction - 1 3/4 is a mixed fraction too.

questions.question: 6 times 1/2 of a pancake equals how many whole pancakes?
questions.explanation: 6 times 1/2 = 6/2. Two halves make one pancake, so 6 halves make 6 ÷ 2 = 3 whole pancakes.

questions.question: 7 times 1/4 = 7/4. Written as a mixed fraction, this is:
questions.explanation: Four quarters make 1 whole; 7 quarters = 4 quarters + 3 quarters = 1 whole and 3/4, i.e. 1 3/4.

questions.question: Which group contains ONLY proper fractions?
questions.explanation: In 4/7, 1/5, 5/11 and 5/8 every numerator is smaller than its denominator. The other groups each contain an improper fraction (9/6, 10/7 or 9/2).

questions.question: From the list 4/7, 1/5, 5/11, 9/6, 5/8, 10/7, 9/2, 1/9 - select ALL the improper fractions shown here.
questions.explanation: 9/6 and 10/7 have numerators bigger than their denominators, so they are improper. 4/7 and 5/8 are proper.

questions.question: Which fraction is the odd one out in 3/5, 14/5, 11/5, 9/5 - and why?
questions.explanation: 14/5, 11/5 and 9/5 all have numerators bigger than 5, so they are improper. Only 3/5 is proper. (11/5 is also above 2, and 3/5 is also below 2, so those reasons are wrong; all four are like fractions.)

questions.question: Fractions that have the SAME denominator are called:
questions.explanation: Like fractions share one denominator, e.g. 3/14, 6/14, 15/14. Different denominators make unlike fractions; unit fractions have numerator 1.

questions.question: Which pair shows UNLIKE fractions?
questions.explanation: 5/14 and 2/8 have different denominators (14 and 8), so they are unlike. The other pairs both have denominator 14 - like fractions.

questions.question: The book describes 3/5 and 2/5 as:
questions.explanation: Both numerators are smaller than 5 (proper) and both denominators are 5 (like). A fraction can be classified both ways at the same time.

questions.question: Unit fractions are always proper fractions.
questions.explanation: True. A unit fraction has numerator 1 and denominator greater than 1, so the numerator is always smaller - that is exactly what proper means.

questions.question: A unit fraction can never be a like fraction with any other fraction.
questions.explanation: False. 1/5 is a unit fraction AND a like fraction with 2/5 (same denominator). It is unlike with 2/7. Unit fractions can be like or unlike with others.

questions.question: Which fraction is the odd one out in 2/21, 5/21, 21/21, 7/21 - and why?
options: 21/21 - the only one equal to a whole
questions.explanation: 21/21 has numerator equal to denominator, so it is improper and equals 1 whole; the others are proper. All four share denominator 21, so none is 'unlike', and 2/21 is not a unit fraction.

questions.question: Statement (I): Fractions having the same denominator are proper fractions. Statement (II): A fraction having one as the denominator is a unit fraction. Select the correct option.
questions.explanation: Same denominator makes fractions LIKE, not proper (15/14 and 3/14 are like but 15/14 is improper). A unit fraction has 1 as its NUMERATOR, not denominator. Both statements are false.

questions.question: Which description of 1/5 matches the book?
options: Unit fraction, unlike with 2/5, like with 2/7
Unit fraction, like with 2/5, unlike with 2/7
questions.explanation: 1/5 has numerator 1 so it is a unit fraction. It shares denominator 5 with 2/5 (like) but not with 2/7 (unlike).

questions.question: A shaded picture shows seven one-thirds. Written as an improper fraction and then as a mixed fraction, 7/3 equals:
questions.explanation: 3 one-thirds make 1 whole, 6 one-thirds make 2 wholes, and 1 one-third is left over. So 7/3 = 2 1/3. Check: 7 ÷ 3 = 2 remainder 1.

questions.question: Convert 13/4 to a mixed fraction.
questions.explanation: Divide 13 by 4: quotient 3, remainder 1 (3 × 4 = 12). The quotient is the whole part, the remainder is the new numerator, and the denominator stays 4: 3 1/4.

questions.question: Convert 19/5 to a mixed fraction.
Convert 44/7 to a mixed fraction.
Convert 125/13 to a mixed fraction.
questions.explanation: 13 × 9 = 117 and 13 × 10 = 130 is too big, so the quotient is 9. Remainder = 125 - 117 = 8. So 125/13 = 9 8/13.

questions.question: When converting an improper fraction to a mixed fraction, the REMAINDER of the division becomes the:
questions.explanation: Steps: divide numerator by denominator; the QUOTIENT is the whole number part; the REMAINDER becomes the numerator; the denominator stays the same (Q R/D).

questions.question: Convert 232/19 to a mixed fraction.
questions.explanation: 19 × 12 = 228 and 19 × 13 = 247 is too big, so the quotient is 12. Remainder = 232 - 228 = 4. So 232/19 = 12 4/19.

questions.question: 19/9 written as a mixed fraction is 2 2/9.
Convert 2 3/4 to an improper fraction.
questions.explanation: Multiply the whole by the denominator and add the numerator: 2 × 4 + 3 = 11. Keep denominator 4: 11/4. (9/4 forgets to add properly; 14/4 wrongly multiplies 2 × 7.)

questions.question: Convert 3 5/9 to an improper fraction.
questions.explanation: 3 × 9 = 27; 27 + 5 = 32. So 3 5/9 = 32/9. 27/9 skips adding the 5 and 17/9 wrongly uses 3 + 5 + 9.

questions.question: Convert 19 5/7 to an improper fraction.
When converting a mixed fraction to an improper fraction, which step comes FIRST?
options: Multiply the whole number by the denominator
Add the numerator to the whole number first
Divide the numerator by the denominator first
Add the two denominators together first
questions.explanation: Step 1: multiply the whole number part by the denominator. Step 2: add the numerator to get the new numerator. Step 3: keep the denominator the same.

questions.question: Statement (I): The fraction 4/2 represents 2 whole units. Statement (II): When 4/2 is converted to a mixed fraction, the remainder is zero, which means there is no fractional part. Select the correct option.
questions.explanation: 4 ÷ 2 = 2 with remainder 0, so 4/2 is exactly 2 wholes and has no fractional part. Both statements are true.

questions.question: A student writes 2 1/3 = (2 + 1)/3 = 3/3. What is the CORRECT improper fraction for 2 1/3?
questions.explanation: You must MULTIPLY the whole by the denominator first: 2 × 3 = 6, then add 1 to get 7. So 2 1/3 = 7/3, which is seven one-thirds - clearly more than 3/3 = 1.

questions.question: Fractions that represent the same portion of the whole are called:
questions.explanation: 'Equivalent' means 'the same' or 'of equal value'. 1/2, 2/4 and 4/8 all cover the same part of a whole, so they are equivalent fractions.

questions.question: You fold a strip in half and colour one half (1/2). Then you fold each half in half again. What fraction of the strip is coloured now?
questions.explanation: The coloured half now shows as 2 of the 4 equal parts, so the fraction is 2/4 - the SAME portion as 1/2. Folding again would show it as 4/8.

questions.question: To make an equivalent fraction, you multiply (or divide) the numerator and the denominator by:
questions.explanation: Both numerator and denominator must be multiplied or divided by the SAME non-zero number, e.g. 2/5 = (2 × 3)/(5 × 3) = 6/15. Zero is not allowed.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: 6/30 = ?/15
questions.explanation: 30 ÷ 2 = 15, so divide the numerator by 2 as well: 6 ÷ 2 = 3. 6/30 = 3/15.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: 16/36 = 4/?
Write the equivalent fraction of 48/36 with numerator 12.
questions.explanation: 48 ÷ 4 = 12, so divide 36 by 4 too: 36 ÷ 4 = 9. 48/36 = 12/9 (an improper fraction stays improper).

questions.question: A pizza is cut into 8 equal pieces and 2 are eaten (2/8). Which set shows three equivalent fractions for the eaten part?
questions.explanation: 2/8 ÷ 2 = 1/4; 2/8 × 2 = 4/16; 2/8 × 4 = 8/32. The other sets break the 'same number on top and bottom' rule (e.g. 2/16 is half of 2/8).

questions.question: Statement (I): The fractions 2/4 and 3/6 are equivalent. Statement (II): For fractions to be equivalent, the numerator and denominator must be multiples or factors of each other. Select the correct option.
questions.explanation: 2/4 and 3/6 both equal 1/2, so (I) is true. (II) is false - 2/6 and 3/9 are equivalent even though 2 is not a factor of 3; what matters is that both are the same portion of the whole.

questions.question: Statement (I): The fractions 6/15 and 3/5 are equivalent. Statement (II): Equivalent fractions represent equal parts of a whole. Select the correct option.
questions.explanation: 3/5 × 3 = 9/15, not 6/15 (and 6/15 ÷ 3 = 2/5). So (I) is false. (II) is the very definition of equivalent fractions, so it is true.

questions.question: 2/6 and 3/9 are equivalent fractions even though 2 is not a factor of 3.
questions.explanation: True. 2/6 ÷ 2 = 1/3 and 3/9 ÷ 3 = 1/3, so both are the same portion. The book uses exactly this pair to show numerators need not be multiples of each other.

questions.question: Select ALL the fractions equivalent to 1/3.
questions.explanation: 1/3 × 3 = 3/9 and 1/3 × 2 = 2/6. 2/3 is twice as big and 3/6 equals 1/2. The book's flower picture (one third red, two sixths pink, three ninths blue) shows these are the same share.

questions.question: To compare LIKE fractions, which numbers do we compare?
questions.explanation: Like fractions already share the denominator, so the one with the greater numerator is greater: 3/4 > 1/4 because 3 > 1.

questions.question: Which is greater, 3/4 or 1/4 - and why?
options: They are equal, because the denominators match
questions.explanation: Same denominator (4) means the pieces are the same size, so more pieces (3) is more: 3/4 > 1/4. Equal denominators do NOT make fractions equal.

questions.question: Arrange 9/12, 2/12 and 5/12 in ascending order.
questions.explanation: Same denominator, so order by numerators: 2 < 5 < 9. Ascending means smallest first: 2/12, 5/12, 9/12.

questions.question: Arrange 7/18, 12/18 and 9/18 in ascending order.
questions.explanation: Compare numerators: 7 < 9 < 12. So ascending order is 7/18, 9/18, 12/18.

questions.question: Arrange 48/84, 44/84 and 49/84 in DESCENDING order.
questions.explanation: Descending means biggest first. Numerators: 49 > 48 > 44, so 49/84, 48/84, 44/84.

questions.question: Neha uses 4/5 cup of butter and Nikhil uses 6/5 cup. Who uses more?
questions.explanation: Both amounts are in fifths, so compare numerators: 6 > 4, Nikhil uses more. In fact 6/5 is more than one whole cup.

questions.question: Shivam ran 3/4 km and Shobhit ran 2/4 km. Who ran farther, and by how much?
questions.explanation: 3/4 > 2/4 because 3 > 2, so Shivam ran farther. Difference = 3/4 - 2/4 = 1/4 km.

questions.question: Statement (I): 2/11 < 9/11 because in like fractions the same whole is divided into as many parts as the NUMERATOR. Statement (II): 2/11 < 9/11 because in like fractions the same whole is divided into as many parts as the DENOMINATOR. Select the correct option.
questions.explanation: The denominator (11) tells how many equal parts the whole has; the numerator counts parts taken. Since the pieces are equal, 2 pieces < 9 pieces. (I) gives the wrong reason; (II) is correct.

questions.question: Imagine 1/2, 1/3 and 1/6 of the SAME chocolate bar. Which is the biggest share?
questions.explanation: Cutting the bar into fewer pieces gives bigger pieces. Halves (2 pieces) are bigger than thirds (3 pieces), which are bigger than sixths (6 pieces). So 1/2 is the biggest share.

questions.question: For unit fractions, the one with the BIGGER denominator is the greater fraction.
questions.explanation: False. A bigger denominator means the whole is cut into MORE pieces, so each piece is SMALLER: 1/6 < 1/3 < 1/2.
Add the numerators: 1 + 3 = 4. The denominator stays 6: 4/6. Never add the denominators (that gives the wrong 4/12).

questions.question: When adding like fractions, what happens to the denominator of the sum?
options: It is added to the sum
questions.explanation: Only the numerators are added. The denominator of the sum remains the same as the denominator of the fractions being added.
3 + 1 + 9 = 13, so the sum is 13/13 - which is exactly 1 whole. The denominator stays 13 throughout.
Subtract numerators: 59 - 23 = 36. Keep the denominator: 36/65. 82/65 adds instead of subtracting.
6 + 21 + 9 = 36; denominator stays 19: 36/19. This is an improper fraction (1 17/19) - a sum of fractions can exceed 1.

questions.question: To add 2/3 + 1/3 on a picture of 9 triangles, you shade 6 triangles for 2/3 and 3 more for 1/3. The sum is:
questions.explanation: 2/3 + 1/3 = 3/3 = 1 whole - all 9 triangles end up shaded. (6 of 9 triangles = 2/3 and 3 of 9 = 1/3, as the answer key notes.)

questions.question: 8/11 - 3/11 = 5/0, because the denominators cancel each other out.
questions.explanation: False. Denominators never cancel - they stay the same. 8/11 - 3/11 = (8 - 3)/11 = 5/11.

questions.question: A student writes 3/8 + 2/8 = 5/16. What is the CORRECT sum?
questions.explanation: Add only the numerators (3 + 2 = 5) and keep the denominator 8: 5/8. Adding the denominators (8 + 8 = 16) is the classic mistake.

questions.question: To subtract like fractions, subtract the numerators and keep the denominator the same.
questions.explanation: True. For example 9/16 - 2/16 = (9 - 2)/16 = 7/16. The denominator of the difference stays 16.

questions.question: Joy drove 6/8 of the distance and Jaya drove 2/8. Who drove more, and by how much?
questions.explanation: 6/8 > 2/8 because 6 > 2, so Joy drove more. Difference: 6/8 - 2/8 = 4/8 of the distance.

questions.question: Ajit jogged for 3/4 hour on Sunday and 1/4 hour on Monday. For how long did he jog in total?
questions.explanation: 3/4 + 1/4 = 4/4 = 1 whole hour. (2/4 hour is how much MORE he jogged on Sunday than Monday.)

questions.question: Riya uses 7/18 of her pocket money for a story book and 5/18 for paints. What fraction is LEFT with her?
Anita ate 2/7 of a cake and her brother Rohit ate 4/7 of the same cake. How much was eaten and how much is left?
questions.explanation: Eaten: 2/7 + 4/7 = 6/7. Whole cake = 7/7, so left = 7/7 - 6/7 = 1/7. Denominators are never added.

questions.question: Sneha uses 5/7 cup of flour for one cake. How much flour does she need for 3 cakes?
questions.explanation: 5/7 + 5/7 + 5/7 = 15/7 cups. Convert: 15 ÷ 7 = 2 remainder 1, so 15/7 = 2 1/7 cups.

questions.question: A farmer planted 6/16 of his field with maize and 4/16 with jowar. What fraction of the field is UNPLANTED?
questions.explanation: Planted: 6/16 + 4/16 = 10/16. Whole field = 16/16. Unplanted = 16/16 - 10/16 = 6/16. (2/16 is how much more maize than jowar.)

questions.question: Body composition: muscle 5/20, fat 2/20, bone 1/20 - the rest is water. What fraction of the body is water?
questions.explanation: Fat + bone + muscle = 5/20 + 2/20 + 1/20 = 8/20. The whole body is 20/20, so water = 20/20 - 8/20 = 12/20.

questions.question: A canteen sends 4/15 of its previously wasted food to an NGO and saves another 7/15 through awareness campaigns. What fraction is STILL wasted?
questions.explanation: No longer wasted: 4/15 + 7/15 = 11/15. Still wasted = 15/15 - 11/15 = 4/15.

questions.question: To find 'what is left' from a whole when the parts are in twentieths, first write the whole as 20/20.
questions.explanation: True. The book does exactly this for body composition: whole = 20/20, so water = 20/20 - 8/20 = 12/20. Writing 1 as n/n makes it a like fraction you can subtract from.

questions.topic: Fractions Around Us and in History
questions.question: The Earth's surface is about 7/10 water and 3/10 land. Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: The chart in the book shows Water 7/10 and Land 3/10. Together 7/10 + 3/10 = 10/10 = the whole surface.

questions.topic: Fractions Around Us and in History
questions.question: Of all the water on Earth, 97/100 is ocean water. What fraction is fresh water (rivers, lakes, soil, ice caps, atmosphere)?
questions.explanation: Whole = 100/100. Fresh water = 100/100 - 97/100 = 3/100. Keep hundredths - 3/10 would be ten times too much.

questions.topic: Fractions Around Us and in History
questions.question: Land use chart: Deserts 19/100, Mountains 15/100, Grasslands 26/100, Forests 31/100, Urban & Rural 9/100. Which has the largest share?
questions.explanation: All are hundredths (like fractions), so compare numerators: 31 is the greatest, so Forests (31/100) have the largest share. Check: 19 + 15 + 26 + 31 + 9 = 100.

questions.topic: Fractions Around Us and in History
questions.question: According to the book, the earliest recorded use of fractions comes from:
questions.explanation: The book's history box says the earliest recorded use of fractions comes from Ancient Egypt, 2000 BCE, where fractions divided food, land and wages fairly.

questions.topic: Fractions Around Us and in History
questions.question: How did the ancient Egyptians write every fraction?
options: As a sum of unit fractions
questions.explanation: Egyptians used only unit fractions, so every fraction was expressed as a sum of unit fractions (like 3/5 = 1/5 + 1/5 + 1/5), with special symbols for 1/2, 1/3, 1/4 and 1/10.

questions.question: Which of these lists ALL the prime numbers less than 25?
questions.explanation: Primes have exactly two factors. 1 is not prime, 9 = 3 × 3 and 21 = 3 × 7 are composite. The primes below 25 are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23.

questions.question: What is the sum of the 5th multiple of 10 and the 4th multiple of 7?
questions.explanation: 5th multiple of 10 = 50; 4th multiple of 7 = 28. Sum = 50 + 28 = 78.

questions.question: What is the difference between the smallest 3-digit number and the largest factor of 9?
questions.explanation: Smallest 3-digit number = 100; the largest factor of 9 is 9 itself. 100 - 9 = 91.

questions.question: Rahul has 18 marbles and wants packets with an equal number in each. Select ALL the packets he can make.
questions.explanation: 6 × 3 = 18 and 3 × 6 = 18 use all the marbles exactly. 2 × 10 = 20 and 8 × 4 = 32 need more marbles than he has.

questions.question: Which numbers have 64, 32 and 96 all as their multiples?
questions.explanation: These are the common factors of 64, 32 and 96: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32. 64 and 96 are not factors of 32, and 3 does not divide 64.
